Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The main room was quiet when I arrived, but the receiving door had been open for a delivery and the floor near the scale was damp. I put the clipboard on the counter by the red marker and checked the date against the sheet from Tuesday. The date was right, and the shift lead had written her initials in the upper corner. The paper copy is still useful because the tablet battery has been unreliable since the update, and people keep trying to enter figures before the page has finished loading.

In produce, we had eleven crates of yellow onions, and four of the crates were from Cedar Farm, while the other seven came from the market wholesaler. The labels were attached, but one was folded under the edge of a crate, so I turned it outward before weighing the contents. The apples were separated into six bins, and the soft fruit bin had pears, peaches, and two trays of plums. The pear count is an estimate because several members took individual pears during the tasting table, and nobody had written down how many. Uh-huh, that is the same issue Marta mentioned at the staff check-in, but this time the tasting did have a sign beside it. The sign said, “Take one piece and leave the rest for Saturday boxes.” The herb bunches were in a cooler and still looked fresh, though the parsley band on the smallest bunch had come loose.

The dry goods shelves need a closer count than the produce shelves because we sell some items by weight and some by package. I counted twenty-eight bags of brown rice, nine bags of red lentils, and thirteen jars of sunflower butter. The two jars with damaged labels are included in the thirteen because the lids and seals are intact, but I made a separate note so the packing team can place them toward the front, where members can see the label condition. There are also three open sacks of oats, and I weighed each one rather than copying the printed starting weight. One sack held seven kilograms, another held just over five, and the last held four kilograms. The rolled oats are from the same lot, but the quick oats are not, and the two kinds need to stay on different shelf rows. Well, the invoice lists both as oats, which makes the shelf label less helpful than it should be. I wrote the lot codes next to each weight.

Section two: Inventory by department begins with the walk-in cooler because its temperature log was updated at noon. The display read three degrees Celsius when I checked it, and the wall thermometer agreed. The cooler held two cases of oat milk, one case of plain yogurt, and a tray of local eggs with one cracked egg already removed from its carton. The egg count was twenty-three, not twenty-four. I put the empty shell in the compost pail and left the carton in the marked inspection crate so the closing crew can record the damaged item. The fridge on the retail side contained six tubs of hummus and five tubs of soft cheese, and the soft cheese date is Friday, which is why it is listed first on the rotation card. The back cooler had a different count because one case of milk was reserved for the cooking class.

In the freezer, there were bags of blueberries from North Slope Farms and a smaller row of spinach portions packed by the cooperative kitchen. The freezer door did not shut on the first try because a folded carton was caught behind the lower shelf. I moved the carton onto the dry rack and tested the door twice after that. The seal held with no gap around the edge. The blueberry total is forty-two bags across three cartons, but one carton has a handwritten harvest date that differs from the delivery sheet. I photographed both labels and added a note for Joel to check the receiving file before changing either date. The spinach count is eighteen portions, and the kitchen sheet records twenty, so I left the inventory number at eighteen and attached the kitchen sheet instead of altering it. Actually, the cooks may have used two portions for the lunch special and forgotten to update their page.

For household supplies, I checked the paper products and cleaning materials in the narrow cabinet by the wash station. There were twelve rolls of paper towels, one unopened box of compostable gloves, and a partial box with eight gloves still inside. The partial box is not part of the sealed stock total, but I recorded it so the wash crew will know what is available before the weekend shift. The dish soap bottles were divided between the refill shelf and the locked cupboard, and the labels on the refill shelf showed two different prices, although the contents are the same soap. I did not change either label because the price question belongs with the coordinator. There are four spray bottles of sanitizer, and all four have readable dilution labels. The mop heads are drying on the rack and should not be counted as clean replacement stock until they have been washed again.

The member pickup area had three unclaimed produce boxes from Thursday and two boxes with names written on masking tape. One box said Lee, and the other said Rosalie, but the pickup log showed that Lee had already collected a box at six ten. I asked Priya to check the entry before moving anything, and she found that Lee’s first box was a pantry order rather than a produce pickup. The log is now clearer because she added the word pantry beside that entry. The Rosalie box still matches the pickup sheet and can stay on the lower shelf until the end of the day. The empty crates beside the scale belong to the Saturday order and are not part of the return count, so I marked them with a blue strip of tape rather than writing another number on the crate itself.

The receiving records showed two deliveries from Cedar Farm and one from the wholesaler, and all three receipts were clipped to the invoice board. The driver for Cedar Farm had brought an extra crate of kale that was not on the first copy of the order, but the updated receipt includes it. I counted the kale with the other greens and wrote the added crate on the margin of the inventory page. The wholesaler receipt has a small fuel surcharge that affects the accounting record but not the physical count, so I left the stock totals alone and put the receipt in the folder marked review. The empty glass jars from the kitchen were stacked next to the return bins, and their count is thirty-six. The jars do not belong in the grocery inventory because they are being held for the jam workshop next month.

Before leaving, I read the sheet from top to bottom and checked that every weight or quantity had a unit beside it where needed. The tablet had charged enough to save the figures, but I also placed the paper copy in the blue binder on the second shelf. The note for Joel is clipped to the freezer page, and the damaged egg carton is visible in the inspection crate near the cooler. I told Marta that the pear estimate and the two oat sack weights were the only figures that might need another look. She said the Saturday packers could use the current sheet as long as the cooler items stayed in date order. The delivery door is now closed, the scale is dry, and the red marker is back in its holder by the counter."}]
